source_message.speaker: client
source_message.text:
Hey Larry — I went through the BOM and overall I really like the direction. This is exactly what I was hoping for.

A few thoughts I’d like your input on before we move forward:

• Motors — I’m wondering if 200 RPM might be a bit low for achieving a strong, frothy matcha texture. Do you think it makes sense to increase RPM while still maintaining enough torque for smooth mixing?

• Whisk — would a stainless steel or milk-frother-style head perform better than the resin whisk in terms of consistency, durability, and foam quality?

• Spout — I’d like to stick with the solenoid approach. It’s important that the pour is clean, controlled, and seamless (mix → open → pour) both for texture and the overall visual experience.

• Splash / mess control — this is really important for events. I want to make sure:
– minimal to no splashing during mixing
– smooth, controlled flow from the spout (no sputtering)
– no dripping when the valve is closed
– good sealing so nothing leaks into the base
– some form of splash guard or lip around the bowl if needed

• Cleaning — I’d like the bowls and spout components to be easy to clean or removable if possible.

Everything else looks great to me. Curious to hear your thoughts on these and if you’d adjust anything before we finalize the BOM.

source_message.speaker: client
source_message.text:
That makes sense — I like the idea of having more power and being able to control the speed range.

I think 3000 RPM works as long as we’re not running it at max all the time. Having the flexibility to dial it in for different mixing levels (slow mix vs higher-speed frothing) is actually ideal.

One thing I do want to make sure of with the higher RPM:
• we keep splashing under control
• the mixing stays smooth and doesn’t get too aggressive at higher speeds

So if needed, I’m open to adding a splash guard or dialing in whisk position / bowl depth to make sure it performs cleanly.

Overall I’m good with this direction.
